passage: Leela, you asked how I'm really doing, and my roommate still calls me "Sad Sachin," so here it is. When she ended it in March, I checked her status every hour, like it would tell me something new. I replayed every fight. I was angry, then just empty. Around week three I did what you said and wrote down what we actually fought about. It was never small stuff. She wanted to move abroad right after graduation; I want to stay near my parents in Nagpur. She laughed at my weekend volunteering at the shelter. Seeing it on paper, the breakup stopped feeling like only rejection. It was also information. I muted her, went back to Sunday football, and started sleeping before two. Last week someone from my batch asked me for coffee, and I said, "Sure, but let's actually talk about what matters to us." That's new for me.

qa.q: Where does Sachin want to stay after graduation?
qa.a: Sachin wants to stay near Sachin's parents in Nagpur.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling in the first weeks after the breakup?
qa.a: Sachin felt angry and then empty, checking the ex's status every hour and replaying old fights.

qa.q: What helped Sachin move from hurt to clearer thinking?
qa.a: Writing down what they really fought about showed a clash of values, so the breakup became useful information instead of pure rejection.

qa.q: How might Leela feel hearing that the advice worked?
qa.a: Leela might feel relieved to see a friend recovering, and quietly glad the suggestion helped.

grounding: Shows a young adult recovering from a breakup and starting to choose a partner on shared values.

passage: The poster in the campus health centre's waiting room said, in big friendly letters, "Ask anything. It stays here." Disha sat under it with a folded list in her lap. Keerthana, her roommate, had come along without being asked. "You okay?" Keerthana whispered. Disha nodded. "Kabir and I talked last night. Properly. I told him I'm not ready for more yet, and that when I am, I want us both to be safe and sure." She twisted the paper. "I was scared he'd sulk." "Did he?" "He said, 'Thanks for telling me. We go at your pace, and you can change your mind anytime.'" Keerthana smiled. "That's the whole test, honestly." A nurse called Disha's name. She stood, took a breath, and walked in with her list, the questions she'd been too shy to search for alone.

qa.q: What did the poster in the waiting room say?
qa.a: It said, "Ask anything. It stays here."

qa.q: What was Disha worried about before talking to Kabir?
qa.a: She was scared he would sulk when she said she wasn't ready, and she still twists the paper nervously as she tells the story.

qa.q: Why is Disha's visit to the health centre a sensible step?
qa.a: She takes her questions to a trained person in a private setting instead of guessing, so any later choices are informed and safe.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Kabir's response?
qa.a: Keerthana sees it as a good sign, calling respect for Disha's pace and her right to change her mind the whole test of a partner.

grounding: Shows a young woman stating a boundary, a partner respecting consent, and her seeking reliable sexual health information.

passage: At 1 p.m. the security guard at the insurance office rang Gautam's desk: "Your mother is at reception with a tiffin." Gautam went down, half touched, half mortified. Vandana held out the steel box. "You skipped breakfast. And I phoned your team leader yesterday to ask about your late hours." Gautam's ears burned. He led her to a bench outside the canteen. "Ma, thank you for the food. Really. But calling my team leader makes me look like a child here. If you're worried, ask me. I'll call you every night at nine and tell you honestly how the hours are." Vandana's mouth tightened. "I only worry." "I know. And I want your opinion on something big, whether I should take the Pune transfer. Can we talk on Sunday?" Her face eased. She nodded, and let him carry the tiffin back upstairs alone.

qa.q: Who did Vandana phone about Gautam's late hours?
qa.a: She phoned his team leader.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when his mother arrived with a tiffin?
qa.a: He felt half touched and half mortified, and his ears burned when he heard she had phoned his team leader.

qa.q: What made Gautam's boundary work without a fight?
qa.a: He thanked her first, named the exact problem, offered a nightly call instead, and asked her opinion on the transfer, treating her as an adult partner.

qa.q: What is it like for Vandana when Gautam asks her to stop calling his team leader?
qa.a: At first it stings, and her mouth tightens, but being asked about the Pune transfer reassures her that she still matters in his life.

grounding: Shows a young adult setting a respectful boundary with a parent while inviting her into a more equal relationship.

passage: Chinmay found the photo while clearing his gallery on the Bengaluru metro: him and Darshan at the college canteen, both covered in Holi colour, a year and a half ago. Their last real conversation had been a thumbs-up in April. Now it was July. He typed "hey, long time" and deleted it, feeling faintly guilty. Darshan was in Kolkata now, working night shifts at a call centre; Chinmay had a new job and a flatmate who cooked at midnight. Neither of them had stopped caring. They had just stopped making time. At his stop, Chinmay sent a voice note instead: "Found this. I miss your terrible jokes. Can we fix a call, Sunday mornings, even fifteen minutes?" The reply came that night, a laughing voice note and one line: "Sunday 10. I'll set an alarm."

qa.q: When did Chinmay and Darshan agree to talk?
qa.a: On Sunday at 10, a fixed Sunday morning call.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay delete his first message?
qa.a: He felt faintly guilty about months of silence, and a bare "hey, long time" seemed too thin to fix that.

qa.q: What small step helped restart the friendship?
qa.a: A warm, specific voice note with a shared photo and a short, fixed Sunday call turned vague good intentions into a routine.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel receiving the voice note after months of silence?
qa.a: Darshan probably feels delighted and relieved to be missed, judging by the laughing reply and the promise to set an alarm 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult reviving a friendship that distance and busy schedules had let slide.

passage: Six weeks into her first term at the university in Pune, Disha still ate dinner in the hostel mess with her earphones in, a playlist from home on repeat. On Sundays she called her mother, said everything was fine, then lay on her bunk scrolling through old school photos until the corridor went quiet. One evening a notice on the mess board caught her eye: the trekking club wanted volunteers to carry supplies for a weekend cleanup. She almost walked past. Ritu, the girl from the room opposite, stopped beside her. "I'm going. Scared of going alone, honestly. Come?" Disha took out one earphone. On Saturday they hauled sacks up a muddy slope, laughing when Ritu slipped twice. That night Disha ate dinner with both earphones in her pocket and a seat saved for her.

qa.q: What did the trekking club want volunteers for?
qa.a: To carry supplies for a weekend cleanup.

qa.q: What does Disha's habit of eating with her earphones in suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt lonely and homesick, shutting out the new place with music from home.

qa.q: What step helped Disha start to belong, and why did it work?
qa.a: Saying yes to a shared activity with Ritu gave them a reason to talk and something to laugh about, which is easier than chatting from nothing 🙂

qa.q: What might Ritu's invitation reveal about her own first weeks?
qa.a: Ritu admits being scared to go alone, so she may have felt as lonely as Disha and was glad to find company.

grounding: Shows a first-year student moving from loneliness toward belonging after leaving home.

passage: The sink in the Manchester flat had been full for four days when Bilal finally taped a note to the kettle: "Can we talk tonight? Not angry. Just tired of the dishes 🙏" Emeka read it and came in with two mugs of tea. "Sorry, man. My shifts at the warehouse changed. I'm barely home." Bilal had rehearsed a speech about fairness all afternoon, but it softened. They sat at the wobbly table and listed every chore on the back of the electricity bill. Emeka took the bins and the bathroom, which he could do on his late mornings; Bilal took the dishes on weekdays. For the heating, they agreed to split the bill evenly and set the thermostat somewhere both could live with. Emeka stuck the list on the fridge. "Review in two weeks?" "Deal."

qa.q: Where did Bilal tape his note?
qa.a: He taped the note to the kettle.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling before the talk, and how did it change?
qa.a: He was frustrated and tired of the dishes, rehearsing a speech about fairness, but softened into understanding once Emeka explained the changed shifts.

qa.q: What made their negotiation fair?
qa.a: They listed every chore together, matched tasks to each person's schedule, and agreed to review the plan in two weeks.

qa.q: How does Emeka see the pile of dishes?
qa.a: Emeka feels sorry and a bit embarrassed, and sees it as a result of the new warehouse shifts rather than not caring.

grounding: Shows two roommates sharing chores and a bill through a calm, fair negotiation.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: For three months Ankita had studied for the state exam in the small room above her father's hardware shop in Sitapur. Lately she slept till noon and still woke tired. She stopped going to the temple fair with her cousins, left her plate half full, and told everyone she was "just busy." One night her younger brother Madhav found her sitting in the dark with the book closed. "Didi, you used to shout at me for wasting time. Now you don't even shout." She tried to laugh and started crying instead. "I don't see the point of anything," she said. Madhav sat beside her until she stopped, then woke their mother. The next morning the three of them took the early bus to the district hospital, where a counsellor saw her on the second floor. Ankita held the ticket stub in her fist the whole ride.

qa.q: Where did Ankita study for the state exam?
qa.a: In the small room above her father's hardware shop in Sitapur.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when Madhav found her in the dark?
qa.a: She felt hopeless and exhausted, seeing no point in anything, and her laugh turning into tears showed how much she had been holding in.

qa.q: Which choices made Madhav's response a wise one?
qa.a: He stayed with her until she calmed, woke their mother that same night, and the family went to a counsellor the next morning instead of waiting.

qa.q: How might Madhav have felt noticing that his sister no longer even scolded him?
qa.a: He probably felt worried and unsettled, because her silence was such a change from the sister he knew.

grounding: Shows long exhaustion, withdrawal and hopelessness being noticed and professional help sought early.

passage: At 3:40 a.m. Indu's thumb was still tapping. One more match, she had said at midnight, and at one, and at two. The game dropped a small glittering chest after every win, and she could feel the itch for the next one before the current one ended. In the morning she missed her 9 a.m. lab for the third time that month. Her lab partner Kamal texted, "You alive? Sir asked about you." Indu stared at the message, then at her screen time: nine hours yesterday. Something cold went through her. That afternoon she deleted the game and asked Kamal to change her account password and keep it. By midnight her hand still reached for the phone. So the next day she booked a slot with the college counsellor, and told Kamal the plain truth: "Wake me for lab."

qa.q: How much screen time did Indu's phone show for the day before?
qa.a: It showed nine hours yesterday.

qa.q: What did Indu feel when she saw her screen time?
qa.a: Something cold went through her, a jolt of alarm and shame at how much the game had taken over.

qa.q: Why was seeing a counsellor a wise next step even after deleting the game?
qa.a: Her hand still reached for the phone at midnight, so the pull was stronger than willpower alone, and a professional can help her break the loop.

qa.q: How does Kamal see Indu's missed labs?
qa.a: Kamal seems worried rather than judging, checking in with "You alive?" and passing on that Sir asked about her.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising a gaming dependence loop and taking steps, including professional help, to exit it.

passage:
Raghav: the certificate guy needs names by tonight. 1500 each, looks totally legit
Tejas: I'm out
Raghav: ?? your dad literally said "get the internship line on the CV somehow" 😅
Tejas: he did. still out
Raghav: everyone's doing it. you'll look weak on paper
Tejas: maybe. I made a list last month after the hostel mess fight. three things I won't bend on: no faking anything with my name on it, no talking down to people, and calling home every week even when we argue
Tejas: a fake certificate breaks number one

Raghav: ok that's actually better than mine
Raghav: send me her email?

qa.q: What did Tejas arrange instead of the fake certificate?

qa.q: How can you tell Tejas feels firm rather than unsure about refusing?
qa.a: Tejas answers in short, calm lines like "still out" and explains a list of non-negotiables, which shows steady confidence rather than guilt.

qa.q: What made Tejas's stand stronger than a bare refusal?
qa.a: Tejas had worked out those values in advance and paired the no with a real alternative, the soil lab, so the choice was both honest and useful.

qa.q: Why might Raghav's view shift by the end of the chat?
qa.a: Seeing an honest internship actually offered, Raghav feels a little envious and asks for the professor's email, so the example changes Raghav's plan too.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding a personal non-negotiable against peer and family pressure.

passage: In the empty classroom of the coaching institute, Kavitha sat staring at her mock paper: 38 out of 100, red circles everywhere. "Useless," she muttered. "You're useless. You'll never clear this." Francis, the senior who ran the evening doubt sessions, was stacking chairs. He stopped. "Would you say that to a friend who got this score?" Kavitha frowned. "No. I'd tell her one bad mock isn't the exam." "So tell yourself." She almost rolled her eyes. Instead she picked up a pencil and wrote on the back of the paper: I didn't finish the tax section because I spent too long on question 4. That's fixable. I'm tired, not stupid. Next week, timed practice, 20 minutes a section. Her shoulders came down a little. Francis nodded at the page. "That's the voice that passes exams."

qa.q: What score did Kavitha get on her mock paper?
qa.a: She got 38 out of 100.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she first looked at her paper?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and angry with herself, calling herself useless and sure she would never clear the exam.

qa.q: What changed when Kavitha rewrote her self-talk?
qa.a: It named the real mistake, too long on question 4, and set a practical plan, so it stayed accountable without the cruelty.

qa.q: How does Francis see Kavitha's harsh words?
qa.a: Francis sees them as unhelpful and gently challenges them by asking whether she would speak that way to a friend.

grounding: Shows a student replacing harsh self-criticism with honest, supportive self-talk after failing a mock exam.
